Nuclear Medicine

  • Radioactivity, the emission of high-energy particles, can kill cells by damaging DNA.
  • Radiation can also be medically beneficial to treat cancer.
  • Radiation therapy exposes only a small part of the body to a precise dosage of radiation.

This PET Scan of a Human Liver Highlights Areas of Diseased Tissue

Matter: Elements and Compounds

  • Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass.
  • Mass is a measure of the amount of material in an object.
  • An element is a substance that cannot be broken down into other substances by chemical reactions.
  • All matter is composed of chemical elements.
Text description of this image

The enlarged section of carbon given in the figure shows the element symbol C in uppercase, the atomic number or the number of protons 6 depicted above it, and the atomic mass or the mass of average atom of that element 12.01 depicted below it.

Chemical Composition of the Human Body

Text description of this image

The illustration shows that oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen make up 96% of the human body weight. The composition of these elements shown in the illustration is listed below: Oxygen (O): 65.0%

The illustration shows it in the entire human body from the waist up, including the arms, hands and head.

Carbon (C): 18.5%

The illustration shows it from the waist to the middle of the thighs.

Hydrogen (H): 9.5%

The illustration shows it from the middle of the thighs to just below the knees.

Nitrogen (N): 3.3%

The illustration shows it from just below the knees to the ankles.

A few other elements (from calcium to magnesium) illustrated as corresponding to the feet region are as follows: Calcium (C a): 1.5% Phosphorus (P): 1.0% Potassium (K): 0.4% Sulfur (S): 0.3% Sodium (N a): 0.2% Chlorine (Cl): 0.2% Magnesium (M g): 0.1% The trace elements comprise less than 0.01% of the human body.

The illustration shows the trace elements corresponding to the size of the toes on a foot. The trace elements include Boron (B), Chromium (C r), Cobalt (C o), Copper (C u), Fluorine (F), Iodine (I), Iron (F e), Manganese (Mn), Molybdenum (M o), Selenium (S e), Silicon (S i), Tin (S n), Vanadium (V), and Zinc (Z n).

Atoms

  • Each element consists of one kind of atom.
  • An atom is the smallest unit of matter that still retains the properties of an element.
  • Atoms are composed of subatomic particles.
Text description of this image

The model shows the atomic nucleus at the center of an electron cloud containing two electrons (each with a negative charge). There are four subatomic particles clustered in the atomic nucleus: 2 protons (each with a positive charge) and 2 neutrons (each with no charge).

Chemical Bonding and Molecules

  • Only electrons are directly involved in chemical reactions.
    • The number of electrons in an atom determines the chemical properties of that atom.
    • Chemical reactions enable atoms to transfer or share electrons.
    • These interactions usually result in atoms staying close together, held by attractions called chemical bonds.

Electron Transfer and Ionic Bonding

  • Ions are atoms or molecules that are electrically charged as a result of gaining or losing electrons.
  • Ionic bonds are formed between oppositely charged ions.
Text description of this image

A sodium atom (N a) has two electrons in its inner electron shell, 8 electrons in its second electron shell, and one electron in its outer (3rd) shell. This outer electron is stripped from sodium and added to chlorine.; A chlorine atom (Cl) has two electrons in the inner shell, 8 electrons in the 2nd shell, and 7 electrons in the outer (third) shell.; Having given up an electron, sodium becomes a positively charged sodium ion (N a plus) with 8 electrons in the outer shell. Having received an electron, chlorine becomes a negatively charged chloride ion (Cl minus), and also has 8 electrons in its outer (third) shell.; The attraction between the ions - an ionic bond - holds them together to form sodium chloride (NaCl).

Covalent Bonds

  • A covalent bond forms when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
  • Covalent bonds
    • are the strongest of the various bonds and
    • hold atoms together in a molecule.
Text description of this image

1. Name (molecular formula): Formaldehyde (CH2O) 2. Electron configuration: Shows how outermost electrons participate in chemical bonding

The figure shows an oxygen atom stacked on top of a carbon atom. Below the carbon atom are two small hydrogen atoms. Each hydrogen atom shares a single pair of electrons (2) with the carbon atom; these are single bonds. The oxygen atom shares 2 pairs of electrons (4) with the carbon atom; this is a double bond.

3. Structural formula: Represents each covalent bond (a pair of shared electrons) with a line

The figure shows an O drawn above a C, with two vertical parallel lines representing a double-bond (two pairs of shared electrons) between the O and C. Branching below the C are two single, opposing diagonal lines connecting to two occurrences of the letter H; these diagonal lines represent single bonds (one pair of shared electrons).

4. Space-filling model: Shows the shape of a molecule by symbolizing atoms with color-coded balls

The figure shows atoms as three-dimensional balls. A red atom is fused to the top of a black atom; both are similar in size. Two smaller white atoms are fused to the bottom of the black atom, roughly on the left and right of the lower surface.

5. Ball-and-stick model: Represents atoms with balls and bonds with sticks

Atoms and bonds are represented as three-dimensional balls and sticks. A red atom is joined by a stick to the black atom below it. Two opposing diagonal sticks join the black atom to two white atoms below it.

Hydrogen Bonds

  • A molecule of water (H2O) consists of two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom by covalent bonds.
  • But the electrons are not shared equally between the oxygen and hydrogen atoms.
  • This causes water to be a polar molecule, one with an uneven distribution of charge.
    • The polarity of water results in weak electrical attractions, called hydrogen bonds, between neighboring water molecules.
Text description of this image

The figure shows that a central water molecule forms four hydrogen bonds (dashed lines) to four other water molecules between regions on the water molecules with opposite charges. The O in the central water molecule (slight negative charge) forms hydrogen bonds with hydrogen atoms (slight positive charge) in two other nearby water molecules. The two hydrogen atoms in the central water molecule also each form a hydrogen bond with an oxygen atom in two different water molecules.

Chapter 2 in-class (1)

Chemical Reactions

  • Cells constantly rearrange molecules.
  • Such changes in the chemical composition of matter are called chemical reactions, and include
    • reactants, the starting materials, and
    • products, the end materials.
  • Chemical reactions can rearrange matter but cannot create or destroy matter.

Water and Life

  • Life on Earth began in water and evolved there for 3 billion years before spreading onto land.
  • The abundance of water is a major reason that Earth is habitable.
  • The polarity of water molecules and the hydrogen bonding that results explain most of water’s life-supporting properties.

Key Concepts of Water

  • Cohesion
  • Strong resistance to temperature
  • Water as solvent
Text description of this image

The figure shows that a central water molecule forms four hydrogen bonds (dashed lines) to four other water molecules between regions on the water molecules with opposite charges. The O in the central water molecule (slight negative charge) forms hydrogen bonds with hydrogen atoms (slight positive charge) in two other nearby water molecules. The two hydrogen atoms in the central water molecule also each form a hydrogen bond with an oxygen atom in two different water molecules.

Cohesion

Text description of this image

The figure shows that evaporation from the leaves pulls water upward through the trunk. A colorized scanning electron micrograph at a scale of 150x provides a closer look at this process showing a network of microscopic water-conducting tubes within the tree’s trunk. A corresponding diagram shows a vertical line of water molecules along the wall of one of the microscopic water-conducting tubes in the trunk; cohesion between these water molecules is due to hydrogen bonds between them.

Temperature Moderation

Text description of this image

In liquid water, hydrogen bonds constantly break and re-form. The image shows water molecules moving close together, with hydrogen bonds forming between only some of the adjacent molecules.; In ice, stable hydrogen bonds hold molecules apart, making ice less dense than water. The image shows that water molecules in ice are regularly spaced and farther apart than in liquid water, with water molecules held in a lattice pattern by the maximum number of hydrogen bonds (4) between each adjacent water molecule.

Water as a solvent

Text description of this image

The image shows that a salt crystal is composed of a block of alternating chloride ion and sodium ion. At the edge of the crystal, water molecules surround a sodium ion in solution, with the oxygen atoms in the water molecules oriented toward the sodium ion. Water molecules also surround a chloride ion in solution, but it is the hydrogen atoms in the water molecules that are attracted to the chloride ion.

Acids, Bases, and pH

  • A chemical compound that releases H+ to a solution is an acid.
  • A compound that accepts H+ and removes them from solution is a base.
  • To describe the acidity of a solution, chemists use the pH scale, a measure of the hydrogen ion (H+) concentration in a solution.
  • Buffers minimize changes in pH.
Text description of this image

Increasingly acidic (from 7 towards 0) corresponds with greater H positive concentration. Acidic solutions have higher concentrations of H plus than OH minus ions; neutral solutions have equal concentrations of H plus and OH minus, and basic solutions have higher concentrations of OH minus than H plus. The pH scale with examples is as follows:

pH 0: Acidic; pH 1: Acidic; Battery Acid (between pH 1 and 2); pH 2: Acidic; Lemon juice; stomach acid; pH 3: Acidic; Grapefruit juice, soft drink; pH 4: Acidic; Tomato juice (between pH 4 and 5); pH 5: Acidic; Black coffee (between pH 4 and 5); pH 6: Acidic; Urine; pH 7: Neutral; Pure water; human blood is between pH 7 and 8; pH 8: Basic; Seawater (between pH 8 and 9); pH 9: Basic; pH 10: Basic; Milk of magnesia (between pH 10 and 11); pH 11: Basic; Household ammonia (between pH 11 and 12); pH 12: Basic; Household bleach (between pH 12 and 13); pH 13: Basic; Oven cleaner (between pH 13 and 14); pH 14: Basic

Ocean Acidification by Atmospheric CO2

Text description of this image

A photo shows a coral reef with the process of acidification by atmospheric C O2 superimposed on it. The process shows that carbon dioxide C O2 from the atmosphere enters the ocean, where the reaction C O2 plus H2O (water) resulting in H2C O2 (carbonic acid) takes place.
